# Introduction \label{Introduction}

Investors often treat the choice between large, mid and small cap indexes as a choice about company size. This report argues that it is mainly a choice about economic exposure and about the kind of risk being taken. This report compares the three local size indexes on their structure (sector exposure, concentration and active share against the Capped SWIX), their risk (the realised volatility of their constituents, diversification and GARCH volatility) and their returns (rolling returns, risk-adjusted performance and a stratification of months by rand and global stress).

# Data

Monthly constituent weights for the large, mid and small cap indexes and the Capped SWIX are available from 2007, and daily index returns (J200, J201, J202 and J433) from 2015. The structure analysis therefore covers 2007-2026 and the risk and return analysis 2015-2026. Weights are rescaled to 100% each month, and missing sectors are filled from other months and from the daily constituent file; the remainder, almost entirely older small caps, is labelled unclassified.

# Structure: what the size indexes hold

Figure \ref{sectors} shows that the three indexes are very different bets on the economy. Large caps were about half resources in 2007, shifted towards industrials until around 2016, and are close to 40% resources again today. Mid caps began as an industrials index and have become more balanced, while small caps are concentrated in industrials and, increasingly, property (31% of the index today). Moving down the size spectrum therefore means swapping commodity exposure for locally listed industrial, financial and property businesses, although, as Section \ref{Beyond} shows, locally listed does not mean exposed to the rand.

```{r sectors, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Sector weights of the size indexes \\label{sectors}"}
Plot_Q2_Sectors(Q2_Sector_Mix(Q2_Holdings))
```

Figure \ref{concas} shows concentration with Lorenz curves, which plot the cumulative share of stocks (smallest first) against the cumulative share of index weight; the further a curve bows below the diagonal, the more a few large stocks dominate, as summarised by the Gini coefficient. Large caps were by far the most concentrated index in 2007 (Gini 0.55) but have become much less so (0.44), while mid and small caps have moved the other way (to 0.41 and 0.34). The biggest change came in June 2023, when Richemont (about 22% of the index) left the large cap holdings. The right panel measures how different each index is from the broad market by combining active share against the Capped SWIX, $\frac{1}{2}\sum_i |w_i^{index} - w_i^{SWIX}|$, with tracking error, following the classification of Cremers and Petajisto (cut-offs of 60% active share and 8% tracking error). Large caps have moved into the closet-indexer corner, with an active share of 13% and a tracking error of only 2% in 2026, so they are now close to a replica of the broad market. Small caps are a consistently concentrated bet (active share of about 95% and tracking error of 9-19% a year), while mid caps move between the diversified and concentrated zones as their tracking error rises in turbulent years.

```{r concas, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Lorenz curves (left) and active share vs tracking error against the Capped SWIX (right) \\label{concas}"}
Plot_Q2_Lorenz_ASTE(Q2_Lorenz(Q2_Holdings), Q2_AS_TE(Q2_Holdings, Q2_Rets))
```

# Risk

Figure \ref{constvol} compares the realised volatility of the constituents of each index over time. Outside crises the typical stock is similarly volatile in all three indexes (a median of about 25-35% a year), but in stress small-cap stocks swing the most: during COVID-19 the median small-cap stock reached about 70% volatility, against about 60% for large and mid caps.

```{r constvol, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Realised volatility of index constituents \\label{constvol}"}
Plot_Q2_Const_Vol(Q2_Const_Vol)
```

This raises a puzzle: small-cap stocks are individually at least as volatile as large- and mid-cap stocks (and more so in crises), yet the small cap *index* is the least volatile of the three. Figure \ref{div} resolves it by plotting, for every month, the weighted average volatility of each index's stocks against the volatility of the index itself. The large and mid cap months cluster around the line where the index is half as volatile as its stocks; the small cap months sit close to a quarter to a third, because small-cap stocks are driven by company-specific news and many trade infrequently, so their moves largely cancel out in the index. In crisis months the small cap points move up towards the half-as-volatile line, as their stocks suddenly move together, so their low index volatility understates their true risk.

```{r div, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "Average stock volatility vs index volatility, monthly \\label{div}"}
Plot_Q2_Div_Scatter(Q2_Diversification(Q2_Const_Vol, Q2_Rets))
```

To see what kind of volatility each index faces, the same GJR-GARCH(1,1) model as in Question 1 is fitted and used to draw news impact curves (Figure \ref{newsimpact}): how much next-day volatility rises after a daily shock of a given size and sign. After a 3% fall, large-cap volatility jumps from about 17% to 25% a year, but after a 3% rise it barely moves. Large caps therefore behave like the broad market, with volatility triggered by global sell-offs (a leverage parameter of 0.14 and a symmetric parameter near zero). Small caps start from a much lower base and react strongly in both directions, rising to about 21% after a 3% fall and 17% after a 3% rise, consistent with company-specific and domestic drivers. Volatility shocks are short-lived in all three indexes, with half-lives of 14-17 trading days.

```{r newsimpact, fig.cap = "News impact curves from GJR-GARCH(1,1) fits \\label{newsimpact}"}
Plot_Q2_News_Impact(Q2_News_Impact(Q2_Garch$Fits))
```

# Returns

Rolling 1-year and 3-year returns relative to the Capped SWIX (Figure \ref{rolling}, where each tile is one month) show how the ranking of the indexes changes over time. Large caps beat the Capped SWIX in 88% of 3-year windows, building most of their lead before 2022. Small caps are the most cyclical: they fell furthest into the COVID-19 crash and then led the market by up to 16% a year during the recovery of 2021-2023. Mid caps lagged the Capped SWIX in about two thirds of 3-year windows.

```{r rolling, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Rolling returns relative to the Capped SWIX \\label{rolling}"}
Plot_Q2_Roll_Heat(Q2_Rolling_Returns(Q2_Rets, Years = c(1, 3)))
```

Over the full period (Figure \ref{riskreturn}) large caps returned about 11.0% a year and small caps 10.3%, both ahead of the Capped SWIX (8.7%), while mid caps returned 7.3%. Small caps achieved the best Sharpe ratio (0.25, using STeFI as the risk-free rate) thanks to their low volatility, but also suffered by far the deepest drawdown (-51%), another sign that their measured volatility understates their risk. Mid caps offered the weakest risk-return trade-off.

```{r riskreturn, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Risk and return, 2015-2026 \\label{riskreturn}"}
Plot_Q2_Risk_Return(Q2_Risk_Return(Q2_Rets, STeFI))
```

# Stratification: performance under stress

The analysis identifies the months in the top and bottom 20% of two stress measures, rand volatility (SAVI) and the VIX, and compares each index in those months with its full-sample behaviour, after winsorising daily returns at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Figure \ref{strat} shows the full distribution of monthly returns in each regime as ridgelines. Rand stress is clearly bad for local equities: in the calmest fifth of months for the rand the median monthly return was 1.7-2.9% for every index, but in the most stressed fifth the Capped SWIX fell in 55% of months, and large and small caps did little better. Mid caps held up best, falling in only 38% of rand-stress months with a median return of +1.5%. Global stress raises volatility more than rand stress (by 30-40% against 15-20%), and most for small caps relative to their normal level. Average returns are higher in high-VIX months, but the much wider distributions show that these months contain both the worst falls and the sharp rebounds that follow sell-offs, such as in April-May 2020, so this reflects volatility rather than genuine protection.

```{r strat, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Monthly returns in calm vs stressed months, stratified by rand volatility and the VIX \\label{strat}"}
Plot_Q2_Strat_Ridges(Q2_Strat_Monthly(Q2_Rets, Strat_Months))
```

# Beyond size: the hidden style and currency bets \label{Beyond}

The comparison so far raises a question the data can answer directly: what is an investor really buying when choosing a size index? Applying the same benchmark-relative factor scores and rand-hedge classification used for SafeCore in Question 1 (Figure \ref{hidden}), the answer is that size is largely a proxy for style. Large caps sit close to the benchmark on every factor, mid caps are tilted towards value with weak growth and negative momentum, and small caps are a deep-value bet (+0.86) on stocks with poor recent momentum (-0.43). This helps explain the return results: the mid and small cap indexes hold cheap, out-of-favour stocks, which lagged over a decade led by the large caps, while the strong small-cap recovery of 2021-2023 coincided with the rebound in value stocks after COVID-19.

The currency profile overturns a common assumption. Small caps are not the rand play they are often taken to be: they hold the most pure rand hedges of any index (33%, against 27% for large caps) and the fewest rand plays (10%). Their largest rand hedges are property stocks such as Vukile, Fortress and Resilient, consistent with the offshore property portfolios several local REITs hold, alongside global businesses such as Datatec and Bytes Technology. Mid caps have a currency mix close to the broad market, so their resilience in rand-stress months is not explained by currency hedges. Finally, the local size effect does not mirror the global one: monthly small-minus-large returns are barely correlated with the equivalent spread for MSCI World small and mid caps (a correlation of 0.09). Unlike the volatility studied in Question 1, the relative performance of the local size segments is driven by local factors.

```{r hidden, fig.height = 4.3, fig.cap = "Factor exposures relative to the Capped SWIX (left) and rand-hedge profiles (right) \\label{hidden}"}
Plot_Q2_Hidden_Bets(Q2_FE, Q2_HP)
```

# Conclusion \label{Conclusion}

The size indexes offer very different risk and return profiles. Large caps delivered the strongest returns since 2015 and now closely resemble the broad market, with volatility driven by global sell-offs. Small caps look the safest on paper, with the lowest volatility and the best Sharpe ratio, but this reflects stocks that rarely move together and trade infrequently: in a crisis they move together and suffered the deepest drawdown. Mid caps were the weakest segment over the decade, but held up best in months of rand stress. For an investor, the choice is less about company size than about exposure: large caps for global and resource exposure, mid caps for a value-tilted exposure to local businesses, and small caps for a deep-value bet that is, perhaps surprisingly, the most rand-hedged segment of the market, bearing in mind that their smooth returns hide significant crash risk.
